title: Russia the Disruptor
gist: Laura Mills reviews three books (Haslam's Hubris, Kinzer's Boiling Point, Notte's We Shall Outlast Them) on how post-Cold War U.S. hubris and NATO expansion helped alienate Russia, while arguing both Haslam and Kinzer underplay Ukrainian agency and Moscow's own aggression. Notte's book shows how Russia has evaded Western sanctions via a shadow fleet, third-country trade and a pivot to China and the yuan, producing a more fragmented and violent multipolar order.

themes.theme: Post-Cold War U.S. hubris and NATO expansion

insights.claim: Historian Jonathan Haslam argues that after the Cold War Western Europeans would have accepted a security alliance accommodating Moscow, but Washington doubled down on a NATO status quo of keeping Russia out.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Frames Russia-West hostility as structural and long-dated, implying a durable geopolitical risk premium in Europe.

insights.claim: NATO grew from 12 founding members in 1949 to 32 today, including the 1999 admission of the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary and a 'big bang' of seven more countries in 2004 despite Russian complaints.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Alliance enlargement is the core grievance underlying Russia's security posture and European defense spending.
insights.quote: NATO had just 12 members at its founding in 1949; it now has 32.
insights.locator: How would NATO adapt to this

insights.claim: The reviewer describes James Baker's 1990 'not one inch' eastward assurance to Gorbachev as the start of a 30-year pattern in which each NATO expansion of membership and mission undermined Moscow's perception of its security.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Helps explain why Russian leadership treats NATO proximity as existential, lowering odds of a quick settlement.
insights.locator: While much ink has been spilled

insights.claim: NATO's 1990s Balkan interventions shifted it from a defensive pact toward offensive use, culminating in Russia's complete break with the alliance over the 1999 bombing of Serbia.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Mission creep is a recurring trigger for Russian escalation narratives.
insights.locator: Membership was not the only thing

insights.claim: After the 1998 Russian stock market crash, the West offered IMF loans tied to painful reforms rather than a Marshall Plan, which Haslam and Kinzer see as a missed opportunity that empowered Russian nationalists.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Austerity-for-aid in a crisis can generate long-run political backlash and hostile regimes.

insights.claim: Haslam argues Putin's post-9/11 intelligence assistance and approval of NATO bases in Central Asia was a grand gesture that Washington wasted by reading it as a desperate bid for an ally.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Suggests windows for U.S.-Russia détente have historically been short and easily squandered.
insights.quote: “Putin’s grand gesture … was effectively wasted,” he writes.

insights.claim: Quoting William Burns, Haslam frames Russia as a declining power that, unable to build itself up, seeks to take the United States down a few pegs, making it at least as disruptive as a rising power.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Declining-power disruption implies persistent spoiler behavior in Syria, Ukraine and beyond, not a stable equilibrium.
insights.quote: “[D]eclining powers can be at least as disruptive as rising powers,”
insights.locator: The U.S. push for regime change

themes.theme: Critique of the 'America caused it' narrative

insights.claim: Laura Mills argues both Haslam and Kinzer are overeager to blame Washington and fail to reckon with Ukrainian agency and Moscow's proactive meddling, such as handing out passports in breakaway Georgia and choking energy supplies to Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Energy coercion is a long-standing Russian tool, a reminder for European gas-supply risk.
insights.locator: Both Haslam and Kinzer reach similar

insights.claim: The reviewer says Kinzer commits to pro-Kremlin narratives, including treating eastern Ukrainian separatists as autonomous rather than Russian-funded and armed.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Signals the information battle over the war's origins remains contested in Western discourse.

insights.claim: Mills argues the Soviet collapse created an inevitable European security vacuum in which an increasingly autocratic Russia would view nearby democratization, including in Ukraine, as an existential threat to the Kremlin.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Implies Russia-Ukraine tensions persist regardless of who governs in Washington.
insights.locator: Yet both authors, in their rush

insights.claim: Mills concludes the war was not inevitable, but even with the best intentions the fissures that alienated Russia from the West would have been hard to resolve.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Argues against expecting a durable U.S.-Russia normalization.
insights.locator: Of course, the war in Ukraine

themes.theme: Russia's pre-war dependence on the West

insights.claim: As of 2022 the EU bought 50 percent of Russian oil exports and over 60 percent of its gas exports, and Russia imported one-third of its goods from the EU.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of the trade rerouting since 2022 in global energy flows.
insights.quote: The EU bought 50 percent of Russian oil exports and over 60 percent of its gas exports

insights.claim: Unlike its slow response to the 2014 Crimea annexation, the West after 2022 swiftly imposed price caps on Russian oil insured or shipped by Western providers and banned exports of electronics, luxury items and dual-use goods.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Price-cap regime tied to Western insurance/shipping is the key lever whose effectiveness drives oil market spreads.

themes.theme: Sanctions evasion and economic pivot to China

insights.claim: Russia built a 'shadow fleet' of off-the-books tankers backed by insurers and financiers in Dubai and beyond to evade the Western oil price cap.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Shadow fleet weakens price-cap leverage and keeps Russian barrels in the market, capping oil upside from sanctions.

insights.claim: Russia's share of India's oil imports rose from 3 percent in 2021 to 38 percent in 2023, while exports to China and Turkey also rose.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: India and China are the swing buyers for Russian crude; secondary sanctions on them would be market-moving.
insights.quote: in India alone, Russia’s share of the country’s oil imports increased from just 3 percent in 2021 to 38 percent in 2023

insights.claim: Putin effectively established duty-free trade from third countries such as Turkey and Kazakhstan, allowing European and U.S. products to reach Russia via re-export.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Third-country re-export hubs are enforcement targets and beneficiaries of sanctions-driven trade.

insights.claim: Russia has decoupled from the U.S. dollar by pivoting to Chinese exports and financing, making it significantly more dependent on the yuan.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: A concrete case of de-dollarization that deepens Russian dependence on China rather than creating true independence.

insights.claim: The Russian economy took an initial GDP hit after the invasion and has since stabilized somewhat, but it has not collapsed.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Sanctions alone are unlikely to force a Russian economic capitulation.

themes.theme: Russia's global-south diplomacy and military partnerships

insights.claim: Hanna Notte shows Russia exploits anti-imperialist sentiment in the global south to cast itself as an outsider against a hegemonic West, paying dividends at the U.N. where many Asian and African countries side with it.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Limits the West's ability to build universal sanctions coalitions.

insights.claim: North Korea and Iran have become major providers of munitions and drone technology to Russia, and Russia has expanded its military footprint in the Sahel via mercenary networks.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: An axis of sanctioned states sustaining Russia's war capacity raises the risk of broader conflict linkages.

insights.claim: Russia's war distraction left it unable to save Assad in Syria in 2024 and pushed Armenia and Kazakhstan to hedge toward other partners.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Russia's influence in its near abroad is eroding, opening space for China, Turkey and the West.

insights.claim: Moscow has shored up BRICS as an alternative to Western institutions like the G7, but the bloc's diverse stakeholders have struggled to unite on global issues.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Tempers expectations of BRICS as a cohesive financial or political alternative.

themes.theme: Costs of war and a fragmented world order

insights.claim: Roughly 1 million Russian soldiers are estimated to have been injured or killed in the war and hundreds of thousands of people have left the country.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: Severe human capital losses weigh on Russia's long-run growth potential and labor supply.
insights.quote: roughly 1 million soldiers are estimated to have been injured or killed
insights.locator: While Russia has avoided total breakdown

insights.claim: Mills argues the end of the unipolar world has so far produced a more fragmented, unstable and violent order, with Trump contributing via his Iran gamble, assaults on European allies and a betrayal of Ukraine in the so-called diesel deal with Moscow.
insights.speaker: Laura Mills
insights.so_what: A structurally higher geopolitical volatility regime argues for persistent risk premia in energy and defense.
insights.quote: the end of a unipolar world has so far heralded the rise of a new order that appears more fragmented, unstable, and violent
